subtype: Approach: collects opinions privately before discussion [Revision]
passage:
Tuesday. Ramesh, the manager, sends a message before the planning meeting: "Please email me your honest concerns about the new schedule by tonight. Don't discuss it with others first."
Wednesday. Before the meeting, Ramesh reads eight replies. Hemant, the newest member, wrote: "The Friday deadline clashes with the supplier's holiday." Two of the senior members had not seen it. In the meeting, Ramesh reads out the concerns without names.
The following Monday. The schedule now has a Thursday deadline. Hemant tells a friend at lunch, "I would never have said that in the room with everyone there."

qa.q: How many replies did Ramesh read before the meeting?
qa.a: Ramesh read eight replies before the meeting.

qa.q: What does Hemant feel about sharing the concern in writing?
qa.a: Hemant feels relieved and safer, since Hemant would never have said it in the room with everyone there.

qa.q: What else could Ramesh do to make sure quiet members are heard?
qa.a: Ramesh could ask each person for one written concern before every big meeting, since it keeps seniors' words from shaping the views of others.

qa.q: How might the senior members see the concern from Hemant?
qa.a: Two of the senior members had not seen the clash with the holiday, so may be grateful that it came up before the schedule was fixed.

grounding: A manager asks for written views before the meeting so junior concerns appear without being shaped by senior voices.

subtype: Approach: collects opinions privately before discussion [Revision]
passage: Seema, since you're leading your first team, let me share something from my own start. Your Vasudha Didi learnt it the hard way. At twenty-six, I was made manager of six people. In meetings, I'd share my idea first, then ask, "Thoughts?" The seniors would agree, and the juniors stayed silent. Then one plan failed, and afterwards a junior told me she had known the problem all along. That night I changed my method. Before every planning meeting, I asked each person to email me three lines: what they liked, what worried them, and one question. Private, before anyone spoke. The first time, two juniors raised the same risk about a supplier. We fixed it before the meeting. I've done it ever since.

qa.q: What did Vasudha ask each person to email?
qa.a: Three lines: what they liked, what worried them, and one question.

qa.q: How did young Vasudha feel when the junior said she had known the problem?
qa.a: She felt shaken and regretful, realising her way of running meetings had kept useful worries hidden.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Asking for private written views before the meeting, so juniors could raise worries without being swayed by seniors.

qa.q: How might the juniors in the story have felt about the emails?
qa.a: They probably felt safer and more heard, able to raise concerns without contradicting seniors in front of everyone.

grounding: An elder recalls asking for written views before meetings, so junior members' concerns appear without being shaped by seniors.

subtype: Approach: collects opinions privately before discussion [Revision]
passage: The planning meeting for the warehouse move was on Monday, half the team was on leave until Sunday night, and Saurabh had only one day to gather views. In past meetings, the seniors spoke first and the juniors just agreed. This time Saurabh sent a message to all nine people on Saturday: "Before Monday, please send me privately: your biggest worry about the move, and one idea. Don't read each other's replies." By Sunday night he had eight answers. Jeevan, the newest person, wrote: "The loading dock at the new site can't take the big trucks. I measured it." Three other juniors mentioned the same dock. On Monday, Saurabh opened the meeting with the dock problem. The seniors went quiet. They hadn't known.

qa.q: How many answers did Saurabh get by Sunday night?
How might Jeevan have felt sending that message?
qa.a: Jeevan probably felt nervous as the newest person, but safer writing privately than speaking up in front of seniors.
Private written views before the meeting let juniors raise the dock problem without being shaped by what seniors say.

qa.q: How might the seniors see the dock problem being raised?
qa.a: They were surprised and quiet, likely grateful it came up before the move.

grounding: Under time pressure, a manager collects written views before the meeting, so junior members' concerns surface unshaped by seniors.
